claim: High-resolution structures of filamentous skeletal muscle α-actin (3.37 Å), cardiac muscle α-actin (3.07 Å), ß-actin (2.99 Å), and γ-actin (3.38 Å) in the Mg2+·ADP state with their native post-translational modifications were determined.
source: Here, we report the high-resolution structures of filamentous skeletal muscle α-actin (3.37 Å), cardiac muscle α-actin (3.07 Å), ß-actin (2.99 Å), and γ-actin (3.38 Å) in the Mg2+·ADP state with their native post-translational modifications.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental cryo-EM structures with specific resolution values and states.

claim: The structures revealed isoform-specific conformations of the N-terminus.
source: The structures revealed isoform-specific conformations of the N-terminus that shift closer to the filament surface upon myosin binding, thereby establishing isoform-specific interfaces.
evidence: The manuscript presents structural data showing different N-terminal conformations.

claim: The N-terminus shifts closer to the filament surface upon myosin binding.
source: The structures revealed isoform-specific conformations of the N-terminus that shift closer to the filament surface upon myosin binding, thereby establishing isoform-specific interfaces.
evidence: The manuscript compares bare and myosin-bound actin structures showing N-terminal movement.

claim: Actin isoforms organize into distinct networks that are essential for the normal function of eukaryotic cells.
source: Actin isoforms organize into distinct networks that are essential for the normal function of eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This is a general statement about actin function supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Subtle differences in actin isoform design principles determine the interaction with myosin motors and actin-binding proteins.
source: Despite a high level of sequence and structure conservation, subtle differences in their design principles determine the interaction with myosin motors and actin-binding proteins.
evidence: This is supported by the structural analysis and comparison with previous literature.

claim: Humans express six actin genes in a tissue-specific and developmentally regulated manner.
source: Humans express six actin genes in a tissue-specific and developmentally regulated manner (Kashina, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The six human actin genes can be grouped into four muscle actins and two nonmuscle actins.
source: The gene products are structurally and functionally highly conserved among vertebrates and can be grouped into four muscle actins: skeletal muscle α-actin, smooth muscle α-actin (vascular), cardiac muscle α-actin, smooth muscle γ-actin (enteric), and two nonmuscle actins (ß-actin and γ-actin; Otey et al., 1987; Vandekerckhove and Weber, 1978).
evidence: This classification is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Most cells maintain a defined ratio of actin isoforms with muscle and nonmuscle actins representing the main isoforms in muscle and nonmuscle cells, respectively.
source: Most cells maintain a defined ratio of actin isoforms with muscle and nonmuscle actins representing the main isoforms in muscle and nonmuscle cells, respectively (Kashina, 2020; Otey et al., 1987; Vandekerckhove and Weber, 1978; Kee et al., 2009; Tondeleir et al., 2009; Patrinostro et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Actin isoforms have specific and redundant roles in cells.
source: Actin isoforms have specific and redundant roles in cells and display different biochemistries, cellular localization, and interactions with myosin motors and actin-binding proteins (ABPs; Pollard, 2016; Kashina, 2020; Perrin and Ervasti, 2010; Vedula et al., 2021; Varland et al., 2019; Bunnell et al., 2011; Tondeleir et al., 2012; Baranwal et al., 2012; Diensthuber et al., 2011; Müller et al., 2013; Lee and Dominguez, 2010; Harris et al., 2020; Lappalainen, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The altered expression and mutation of the genes encoding for actin isoforms have been linked to human diseases.
source: The altered expression and mutation of the genes encoding for actin isoforms have been linked to human diseases (Tondeleir et al., 2009; Chaponnier and Gabbiani, 2004; Parker et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Actin isoforms share high sequence identity at the protein level (~93–99%).
source: Actin isoforms share high sequence identity at the protein level (~93–99%) and the propensity to self-assemble into helical, polarized filaments (F-actin) from monomers (G-actin; Pollard, 2016; Perrin and Ervasti, 2010; Dominguez and Holmes, 2011; Arnesen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and is consistent with established knowledge.

claim: Actin isoforms have the propensity to self-assemble into helical, polarized filaments (F-actin) from monomers (G-actin).
source: Actin isoforms share high sequence identity at the protein level (~93–99%) and the propensity to self-assemble into helical, polarized filaments (F-actin) from monomers (G-actin; Pollard, 2016; Perrin and Ervasti, 2010; Dominguez and Holmes, 2011; Arnesen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a well-established property of actin supported by citations.

claim: The first crystal structure of G-actin in complex with DNaseI was published ~30 years ago.
source: Since the publication of the first crystal structure of G-actin in complex with DNaseI ~30 years ago, extensive studies have advanced our understanding of the structure of monomeric and filamentous actin, polymerization mechanisms, post-translational modifications (PTMs), interaction with drugs, myosin motors, and ABPs at ever-increasing resolution (Dominguez and Holmes, 2011; Holmes et al., 1990; Kabsch et al., 1990; von der Ecken et al., 2016; Chou and Pollard, 2019; Zsolnay et al., 2020; Chou and Pollard, 2020; Belyy et al., 2020; Merino et al., 2018; Mentes et al., 2018; Mei et al., 2020; Ducka et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2007; Otomo et al., 2005; Oda et al., 2009; Egelman et al., 1982; Ali et al., 2022; Oda et al., 2020; Gong et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citations.

claim: Isoform-specific mechanisms with myosin motors and ABPs that drive functional distinction are widely described but poorly understood at the structural level.
source: Although isoform-specific mechanisms with myosin motors and ABPs that drive functional distinction are widely described, they are poorly understood at the structural level.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: The Pick-ya actin method was used to recombinantly produce human ß-actin and γ-actin in an engineered Pichia pastoris strain.
source: Specifically, we used our previously established Pick-ya actin method to recombinantly produce human ß-actin and γ-actin in an engineered Pichia pastoris strain that expresses the human N-acetyl transferase NAA80 and histidine methyl transferase SETD3 to ensure uniform Nt-acetylation and methylation of H72/H73, a conserved PTM profile of vertebrate actins (Hatano et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used, supported by a citation.

claim: The engineered Pichia pastoris strain expresses the human N-acetyl transferase NAA80 and histidine methyl transferase SETD3 to ensure uniform Nt-acetylation and methylation of H72/H73.
source: Specifically, we used our previously established Pick-ya actin method to recombinantly produce human ß-actin and γ-actin in an engineered Pichia pastoris strain that expresses the human N-acetyl transferase NAA80 and histidine methyl transferase SETD3 to ensure uniform Nt-acetylation and methylation of H72/H73, a conserved PTM profile of vertebrate actins (Hatano et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the experimental system used.

claim: Nt-acetylation and methylation of H72/H73 is a conserved PTM profile of vertebrate actins.
source: Specifically, we used our previously established Pick-ya actin method to recombinantly produce human ß-actin and γ-actin in an engineered Pichia pastoris strain that expresses the human N-acetyl transferase NAA80 and histidine methyl transferase SETD3 to ensure uniform Nt-acetylation and methylation of H72/H73, a conserved PTM profile of vertebrate actins (Hatano et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and is consistent with established knowledge.

claim: Skeletal muscle α-actin was purified from rabbit skeletal muscle.
source: Skeletal muscle α-actin and cardiac muscle α-actin were purified from rabbit skeletal muscle and the left ventricle of a bovine heart, respectively.
evidence: This describes the source of the protein used in the study.

claim: Cardiac muscle α-actin was purified from the left ventricle of a bovine heart.
source: Skeletal muscle α-actin and cardiac muscle α-actin were purified from rabbit skeletal muscle and the left ventricle of a bovine heart, respectively.
evidence: This describes the source of the protein used in the study.

claim: All actin isoforms are conserved across vertebrates at the protein level.
source: At the protein level, all actin isoforms are conserved across vertebrates, allowing us to compare our structures to previous structures of filamentous actin from other vertebrate species in the correct physiological context (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Pollard, 2016; Perrin and Ervasti, 2010; Dominguez and Holmes, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations and sequence analysis.

claim: The N-termini of bare muscle and nonmuscle actins have different orientations that contribute to distinct binding interfaces for myosin motors and likely other ABPs.
source: Our 2.99–3.38 Å resolution structures of filamentous actin isoforms show that the N-termini of bare muscle and nonmuscle actins have different orientations that contribute to distinct binding interfaces for myosin motors and likely other ABPs.
evidence: This is based on structural data from the study.

claim: The structures show local resolutions ranging from 2.1 to 3.5 Å for skeletal muscle α-actin.
source: The structures show local resolutions ranging from 2.1 to 3.5 Å for skeletal muscle α-actin, 1.9–3.3 Å for cardiac muscle α-actin, 1.5–3.0 Å for ß-actin, and 2.1–4.4 Å for γ-actin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data analysis.

claim: The structures show local resolutions ranging from 1.9–3.3 Å for cardiac muscle α-actin.
source: The structures show local resolutions ranging from 2.1 to 3.5 Å for skeletal muscle α-actin, 1.9–3.3 Å for cardiac muscle α-actin, 1.5–3.0 Å for ß-actin, and 2.1–4.4 Å for γ-actin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data analysis.

claim: The structures show local resolutions ranging from 1.5–3.0 Å for ß-actin.
source: The structures show local resolutions ranging from 2.1 to 3.5 Å for skeletal muscle α-actin, 1.9–3.3 Å for cardiac muscle α-actin, 1.5–3.0 Å for ß-actin, and 2.1–4.4 Å for γ-actin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data analysis.

claim: The structures show local resolutions ranging from 2.1–4.4 Å for γ-actin.
source: The structures show local resolutions ranging from 2.1 to 3.5 Å for skeletal muscle α-actin, 1.9–3.3 Å for cardiac muscle α-actin, 1.5–3.0 Å for ß-actin, and 2.1–4.4 Å for γ-actin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data analysis.

claim: For all actin isoforms, the highest local resolutions were obtained in the central core region.
source: For all actin isoforms, the highest local resolutions were obtained in the central core region.
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data analysis.

claim: Lower local resolutions were obtained in the most surface-exposed and flexible regions such as the N-terminus and the D-loop.
source: Lower local resolutions were obtained in the most surface-exposed and flexible regions such as the N-terminus and the D-loop as expected.
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data analysis and is consistent with expectations.

claim: All actin structures were solved in the Mg2+·ADP state.
source: All actin structures were solved in the Mg2+·ADP state (Figure 1E, Figure 2) and have been obtained without the use of stabilizing drugs that may interfere with the filament structure (Diensthuber et al., 2011; Isambert et al., 1995; Zimmermann et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the nucleotide state of the structures.

claim: The actin structures have been obtained without the use of stabilizing drugs that may interfere with the filament structure.
source: All actin structures were solved in the Mg2+·ADP state (Figure 1E, Figure 2) and have been obtained without the use of stabilizing drugs that may interfere with the filament structure (Diensthuber et al., 2011; Isambert et al., 1995; Zimmermann et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions and is supported by citations.

claim: The superposition of all actin isoform structures shows a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) between 0.83Å to 1.04Å for Cα atoms, indicating an overall similar topology.
source: The superposition of all actin isoform structures shows a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) between 0.83Å to 1.04Å for Cα atoms, indicating an overall similar topology.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison analysis.

claim: No significant differences in the pitch of the actin helix were observed between structures of actin isoforms.
source: No significant differences in the pitch of the actin helix were observed between our structures of actin isoforms, emphasizing their overall conserved filamentous structure in the absence of myosin motors or ABPs.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: Actin isoforms show the largest divergence at the acidic N-terminus within SD1.
source: Actin isoforms show the largest divergence at the acidic N-terminus within SD1 (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on sequence and structural analysis.

claim: There are no substitutions in SD2, the smallest and most flexible subdomain.
source: There are no substitutions in SD2, the smallest and most flexible subdomain (Kudryashov and Reisler, 2013).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and is supported by a citation.

claim: The nucleotide-binding cleft active site is conserved between actin isoforms.
source: Our cryo-EM reconstructions show that the nucleotide-binding cleft active site is conserved between actin isoforms (Figure 1E and Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: The densities for Mg2+ and ADP were assigned without ambiguity.
source: The densities for Mg2+ and ADP were assigned without ambiguity and revealed interactions with amino acids located in SD2 (Q58/Q59 and Y68/Y69) and SD4 (E206/E207, R209/R210, K212/K213, and E213/E214) but also with amino acids located in SD1 (M15/L16, K17/K18, Q136/Q137, and Y336/Y337) and SD3 (D156/D157, M304/M305, Y305/Y306, and K335/K336; Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM density analysis.

claim: Amino acid Y305/Y306 forms π-π interactions with the adenine ring of ADP.
source: While most of the interactions are polar and electrostatic, amino acid Y305/Y306 forms π-π interactions with the adenine ring of ADP.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the active site.

claim: The superimposition of the nucleotide cleft active sites of the four structures of actin isoforms shows small differences in the positions of the nucleotide (RMSD ~0.44–0.47 Å).
source: The superimposition of the nucleotide cleft active sites of our four structures of actin isoforms shows small differences in the positions of the nucleotide (RMSD ~0.44–0.47 Å) and the bound Mg2+ (RMSD ~0.5–1.3 Å), especially in the position of the β-phosphate group relative to the α-phosphate group (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The superimposition of the nucleotide cleft active sites shows small differences in the positions of the bound Mg2+ (RMSD ~0.5–1.3 Å).
source: The superimposition of the nucleotide cleft active sites of our four structures of actin isoforms shows small differences in the positions of the nucleotide (RMSD ~0.44–0.47 Å) and the bound Mg2+ (RMSD ~0.5–1.3 Å), especially in the position of the β-phosphate group relative to the α-phosphate group (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: Amino acid substitution M15/L16 between nonmuscle and muscle actin does not alter the overall topology of the nucleotide-binding site.
source: Amino acid substitution M15/L16 between nonmuscle and muscle actin does not alter the overall topology of the nucleotide-binding site.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The longer side chain of M15 in nonmuscle actins acts as an extended lid that flanks the active site and shields the phosphate groups of ADP.
source: Instead, the longer side chain of M15 in nonmuscle actins, located in a loop that protrudes into the nucleotide-binding cleft, acts as an extended lid that flanks the active site and shields the phosphate groups of ADP (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: Amino acids C10 and V17 in muscle actins are substituted with V9/I9 and C16 in β/γ-actin.
source: Near the nucleotide-binding cleft active site, amino acids C10 and V17 in muscle actins are substituted with V9/I9 and C16 in β/γ-actin (Figure 3, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on sequence and structural analysis.

claim: Reciprocal amino acid substitutions C10/V17 and V9/I9/C16 maintain the overall oxidation-reduction environment within filamentous actin isoforms.
source: These reciprocal amino acid substitutions maintain the overall oxidation-reduction environment within filamentous actin isoforms which is important for its dynamic properties and the interaction with some regulatory proteins (Farah et al., 2011; Lassing et al., 2007; Wilson et al., 2016; Terman and Kashina, 2013).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and is supported by citations.

claim: Longitudinal interactions are mainly mediated by hydrophilic amino acids that are likely to enable interactions with water molecules.
source: The analysis of interprotomer interfaces in our four structures of actin isoforms (Figure 4, Figure 5, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showed that longitudinal interactions are mainly mediated by hydrophilic amino acids that are likely to enable interactions with water molecules that were recently shown to mediate interprotomer contacts within the filament core (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Reynolds et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and is supported by a citation.

claim: Amino acid substitutions at the longitudinal interprotomer interface include L175/M176, T200/V201, Q224/N225, C271/A272, F278/Y279, and V286/I287.
source: Amino acid substitutions at the longitudinal interprotomer interface (also called long pitch helix interface) include L175/M176, T200/V201, Q224/N225, C271/A272, F278/Y279, and V286/I287.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: The transverse interprotomer interface is formed through hydrophilic and hydrophobic interactions.
source: The transverse interprotomer interface (also called short pitch helix interface) is formed through hydrophilic and hydrophobic interactions (Figure 5, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: Most of the transverse interprotomer interactions are direct and not mediated by solvent.
source: In contrast to interactions at the longitudinal interface, most of the transverse interprotomer interactions are direct and not mediated by solvent.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: A single amino acid substitution (V286/I287) is present at the transverse interprotomer interface.
source: A single amino acid substitution (V286/I287) is present at the transverse interprotomer interface.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: Amino acid I287 is in hydrophobic contact with I208 and L242 in muscle actins and buries a surface area of ~113 Å2.
source: Amino acid I287 is in hydrophobic contact with I208 and L242 in muscle actins and buries a surface area of ~113 Å2, whereas the interaction between V286, I207, and L241 in nonmuscle actins is less hydrophobic and buries a surface area of ~83 Å2 in the transverse interprotomer interface (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: The interaction between V286, I207, and L241 in nonmuscle actins is less hydrophobic and buries a surface area of ~83 Å2 in the transverse interprotomer interface.
source: Amino acid I287 is in hydrophobic contact with I208 and L242 in muscle actins and buries a surface area of ~113 Å2, whereas the interaction between V286, I207, and L241 in nonmuscle actins is less hydrophobic and buries a surface area of ~83 Å2 in the transverse interprotomer interface (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: Interactions with the D-loop located in SD2 are conserved in structures of actin isoforms.
source: Interactions with the D-loop located in SD2 are conserved in our structures of actin isoforms, underlining the critical and conserved role of the D-loop to mediate interprotomer interactions.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: At the intersection of the longitudinal and transverse interprotomer interfaces, H39/40 and H172/H173 together with M43/M44 act as central anchors.
source: At the intersection of the longitudinal and transverse interprotomer interfaces, H39/40 and H172/H173 together with M43/M44 act as central anchors.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: The quality of the density maps allowed resolution of both key PTMs (Nt-acetylation and H72/H73 methylation).
source: The quality of our density maps allowed us to resolve both key PTMs (Figure 1E, Figure 1—video 5, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data analysis.

claim: The presence of resolvable density allowed modeling of the entire N-terminus including the Nt-acetylated D1 (D1Ac) and the Nt-acetylated E1 (E1Ac) in the cryo-EM reconstructions of β- and γ-actin.
source: Specifically, the presence of resolvable density allowed us to model the entire N-terminus including the Nt-acetylated D1 (D1Ac) and the Nt-acetylated E1 (E1Ac) in the cryo-EM reconstructions of β- and γ-actin (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data analysis.

claim: The acetylation site on the N-terminus is exposed on the filament surface and adds an additional negative charge to the already negatively charged N-terminus.
source: The acetylation site on the N-terminus is exposed on the filament surface and adds an additional negative charge to the already negatively charged N-terminus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and chemical properties.

claim: There are no resolvable densities for the very N-terminus, including Nt-acetylation, in density maps of skeletal muscle α-actin and cardiac muscle α-actin.
source: Like in previous cryo-EM structures of muscle α-actins, there are no resolvable densities for the very N-terminus, including Nt-acetylation, in our density maps of skeletal muscle α-actin and cardiac muscle α-actin (Figure 1E), possibly due to nonuniform PTM patterns of native, tissue-purified muscle actins.
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data analysis and comparison with previous structures.

claim: The methylated H72/H73 (H72Me/H73Me) was resolved in all cryo-EM reconstructions of actin isoforms.
source: In addition to Nt-acetylation in β- and γ-actin, we could resolve the methylated H72/H73 (H72Me/H73Me) in all cryo-EM reconstructions of actin isoforms (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data analysis.

claim: The presence of both key PTMs in the cryo-EM reconstructions emphasizes that recombinant human actins represent bona fide post-translationally processed, mature nonmuscle actins.
source: The presence of both key PTMs in our cryo-EM reconstructions emphasizes that our recombinant human actins represent bona fide post-translationally processed, mature nonmuscle actins (Hatano et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on the structural data and is supported by a citation.

claim: Myosin motors bind actin in a nucleotide-dependent, reversible manner to generate force and motion.
source: Myosin motors bind actin in a nucleotide-dependent, reversible manner to generate force and motion (Heissler and Sellers, 2016a; Sellers, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The myosin enzymatic cycle can be categorized into states with weak (ATP and ADP·Pi) and strong (ADP and nucleotide-free [rigor]) actin affinity.
source: The myosin enzymatic cycle can be categorized into states with weak (ATP and ADP·Pi) and strong (ADP and nucleotide-free [rigor]) actin affinity (De La Cruz and Ostap, 2009; Heissler and Sellers, 2016b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the strong affinity states, a binding interface is established between actin and the myosin motor domain.
source: In the strong affinity states, a binding interface is established between actin and the myosin motor domain (von der Ecken et al., 2016; Doran and Lehman, 2021; Lorenz and Holmes, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Myosin binding to actin filaments causes subtle conformational changes in the filament.
source: Myosin binding to actin filaments causes subtle conformational changes in the filament (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: Superimposition of the actin structures showed that the Cα of bare and myosin-bound actin protomers deviate with an RMSD of ~1.25–3 Å.
source: Superimposition of the actin structures showed that the Cα of bare and myosin-bound actin protomers deviate with an RMSD of ~1.25–3 Å.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The conformational changes in actin upon myosin binding are similar for myosins from different classes and independent of the nucleotide state of the respective motor domain.
source: These changes are similar for myosins from different classes and independent of the nucleotide state of the respective motor domain (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: SD2 adopts a different conformation in myosin-bound actin compared to bare actin.
source: The superposition of structures of bare actin isoforms and known structures of myosin-bound actins shows that SD2 adopts a different conformation (Figure 6A and B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The conformation of the D-loop differs with a Cα RMSD of ~0.95–1.25 Å between bare and myosin-bound actin.
source: The conformation of the D-loop, located in SD2, differs with a Cα RMSD of ~0.95–1.25 Å (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: Superimposition of bare γ-actin with γ-actin/NM2C complex shows the subtle inward movement of the D-loop with a Cα RMSD of ~1.25 Å in the myosin-bound state.
source: Superimposition of bare γ-actin with γ-actin/NM2C complex shows the subtle inward movement of the D-loop with a Cα RMSD of ~1.25 Å in the myosin-bound state, suggesting that myosin-binding induces subtle changes in the barbed end groove that do not change the separation between SD1/SD3 and SD2/SD4.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The inward movement of the D-loop (RMSD ~0.91 Å) is also observed in the structure of cardiac myosin bound to the thin filament compared to the structure of bare cardiac muscle α-actin.
source: The inward movement of the D-loop (RMSD ~0.91 Å) is also observed in the recent structure of cardiac myosin bound to the thin filament compared to our structure of bare cardiac muscle α-actin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that myosin and not the regulatory proteins tropomyosin and troponin drive this structural change.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The D-loop conformation does not change significantly with respect to the nucleotide states (rigor versus ADP) of the compared myosins.
source: The analysis of the actomyosin interface also shows that the D-loop conformation does not change significantly with respect to the nucleotide states (rigor versus ADP) of the compared myosins (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The superimposition of bare and myosin-bound actin structures shows that the N-termini of skeletal muscle α-actin points in a different direction compared to those from ß-actin and γ-actin.
source: The superimposition of bare and myosin-bound actin structures shows that the N-termini of skeletal muscle α-actin points in a different direction compared to those from ß-actin and γ-actin (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The actin N-terminus is positioned closer to the filament surface in myosin-bound structures compared to bare actin structures.
source: The actin N-terminus is positioned closer to the filament surface in myosin-bound structures compared to our bare actin structures (Figure 7, Figure 6—video 1, Figure 7—video 1).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The negatively charged N-termini of bare ß-actin and γ-actin are near loop-2, a major element of the actomyosin interface that is rich in positively charged amino acids and variable in length.
source: The negatively charged N-termini of bare ß-actin and γ-actin are near loop-2, a major element of the actomyosin interface that is rich in positively charged amino acids and variable in length (Heissler and Manstein, 2011; Joel et al., 2001; Murphy and Spudich, 1999; Uyeda et al., 1994).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and is supported by citations.

claim: The interface between the actin N-terminus and myosin loop-2 is likely to represent one of the initial contact sites upon the formation of a transient intermediate between both proteins during the formation of the actomyosin complex.
source: This interface is likely to represent one of the initial contact sites upon the formation of a transient intermediate between both proteins during the formation of the actomyosin complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: Nt-acetylation of actin likely enhances long-range electrostatic interactions between actin and myosin that subsequently trigger allosteric structural changes.
source: Nt-acetylation of actin likely enhances long-range electrostatic interactions between both proteins that subsequently trigger allosteric structural changes that result in the formation of the actomyosin interface as suggested previously (Abe et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis and is supported by a citation.

claim: A cluster of positively charged amino acids (R661, R663, and R664) in loop-2 of NM2C may interact with either the acetylated N-terminus of ß-actin (D1Ac, D2, and D3) or the acetylated N-terminus of γ-actin (E1Ac, E2, and E3) to stabilize the interface.
source: Furthermore, we observed a cluster of positively charged amino acids (R661, R663, and R664) in loop-2 of NM2C that may interact with either the acetylated N-terminus of ß-actin (D1Ac, D2, and D3) or the acetylated N-terminus of γ-actin (E1Ac, E2, and E3; Figure 7B–C) to stabilize the interface.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: A shorter loop-2, as it is found in M1B, is less efficient in stabilizing the actin N-terminus due to geometric constraints that limit its ability to pull the N-terminus closer to the filament surface in the strong binding states compared to a longer loop-2 as it is found in NM2C.
source: We also showed that a shorter loop-2, as it is found in M1B, is less efficient in stabilizing the actin N-terminus due to geometric constraints that limit its ability to pull the N-terminus closer to the filament surface in the strong binding states compared to a longer loop-2 as it is found in NM2C (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: Distinct actin-myosin interfaces are formed between actin isoforms and myosin motor proteins that may determine the strength of the interaction and biochemical outputs.
source: This suggests that distinct actin-myosin interfaces are formed between actin isoforms and myosin motor proteins that may determine the strength of the interaction and biochemical outputs.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: The overall structure of actin isoforms is conserved, as expected from the high-sequence conservation.
source: The overall structure of actin isoforms is conserved, as expected from the high-sequence conservation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and sequence comparison.

claim: Minor differences were observed near the nucleotide-binding cleft that may contribute to the reported differences in the biochemistries of actin isoforms.
source: However, each structure shows subtle but defining differences. Minor differences were observed near the nucleotide-binding cleft (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) that may contribute to the reported differences in the biochemistries of actin isoforms (Chen et al., 2021; Bergeron et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and is supported by citations.

claim: The transverse interface is more conserved compared to the longitudinal interprotomer interface.
source: The comparison of longitudinal and transverse interprotomer interfaces revealed that the transverse interface is, with only one amino acid substitution (V286/I287), more conserved compared to the longitudinal interprotomer interface which features several amino acid substitutions (L175/M176, T200/V201, Q224/N225, C271/A272, F278/Y279, and V286/I287; Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D, Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: Conserved amino acids (H39/H40, H172/H173, and M43/M44) at the intersection of the longitudinal and transverse interprotomer interfaces are highly susceptible to oxidative stress caused by reactive oxygen species.
source: These residues were previously shown to be highly susceptible to oxidative stress caused by reactive oxygen species and suggest a possible implication for the filament stability of actin isoforms (Varland et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The absence of amino acid substitutions in SD2 and conserved interactions between the SD2 D-loop and amino acids of SD1 and SD3 suggests selective pressure to maintain this critical structural element.
source: The absence of amino acid substitutions in SD2 and conserved interactions between the SD2 D-loop and amino acids of SD1 and SD3 suggests selective pressure to maintain this critical structural element.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: The D-loop of actin isoforms is located closer to the filament surface in myosin-bound structures compared to structures of bare actin filaments.
source: We also noticed that the D-loop of actin isoforms is located closer to the filament surface in myosin-bound structures compared to structures of bare actin filaments.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The most prominent structural change between bare actin isoforms corresponds to the N-terminus location.
source: The most prominent structural change between bare actin isoforms corresponds to the N-terminus location (Figure 1, Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: The different conformations of the N-terminus between muscle and nonmuscle actins contribute to the formation of actin isoform-specific interfaces with myosin motors involving a more subtle movement of the N-terminus rather than a large-scale pulling mechanism.
source: Based on our structures that show different conformations of the N-terminus between muscle and nonmuscle actins, we suggest that instead of a large conformational change through a pulling mechanism, actin isoform-specific interfaces with myosin motors are formed that involve a more subtle movement of the N-terminus.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison.

claim: Different interfaces between actin isoforms and myosin motors together with the subtle differences in the amino acid sequence of the N-terminus region are likely to contribute to the extent actin isoforms can activate the enzyme function of myosin motors in vitro and in cells.
source: These different interfaces together with the subtle differences in the amino acid sequence of the N-terminus region are likely to contribute to the extent actin isoforms can activate the enzyme function of myosin motors in vitro and in cells (Müller et al., 2013; Lappalainen, 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis and is supported by citations.

claim: Most cells maintain multiple actin isoforms and a defined complement of myosin motors.
source: In fact, most cells maintain multiple actin isoforms and a defined complement of myosin motors (Kashina, 2020; Otey et al., 1987; Sellers, 2000; Heissler and Sellers, 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Cell type-specific mixing and matching of actin isoforms and myosin motors is likely to fine-tune the enzymatic output of myosin motors for specialized functions.
source: This cell type-specific mixing and matching is likely to fine-tune the enzymatic output of myosin motors for specialized functions (Kee et al., 2009; Müller et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations.

claim: Previous in vitro experiments with recombinant proteins revealed isoform-specific differences in the interaction between muscle and nonmuscle actin isoforms and individual myosin motors.
source: For example, previous in vitro experiments with recombinant proteins revealed isoform-specific differences in the interaction between muscle and nonmuscle actin isoforms and individual myosin motors (Müller et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Predominantly nonsarcomeric myosins have a faster ATPase activity and in vitro sliding velocity when assayed with nonmuscle actins compared to muscle actin.
source: Notably, predominantly nonsarcomeric myosins have a faster ATPase activity and in vitro sliding velocity when assayed with nonmuscle actins compared to muscle actin, suggesting selective fine-tuning of the functional competencies of myosin-actin combinations with implications for cell function (Müller et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The biochemical properties of the very N-terminus of actin isoforms are key contributors to the formation of isoform-specific interfaces with myosin motors.
source: Based on our structural and previous biochemical studies, we speculate that the biochemical properties of the very N-terminus of actin isoforms are key contributors to the formation of isoform-specific interfaces with myosin motors (Müller et al., 2013; Cook et al., 1993; Abe et al., 2000).
evidence: This is speculation based on structural analysis and is supported by citations.

claim: The very N-termini of mature β-actin (DDD) and γ-actin (EEE) have different pKa values, resulting in a higher negative electron charge density in β-actin compared to γ-actin.
source: For instance, the very N-termini of mature β-actin (DDD) and γ-actin (EEE) have different pKa values, resulting in a higher negative electron charge density in β-actin compared to γ-actin that is further increased by Nt-acetylation in both isoforms.
evidence: This is based on chemical properties and structural analysis.

claim: Differences in charge density at the N-terminus are likely to contribute to distinct interactions with the positively charged loop-2 and other actin-binding elements in the motor domain of myosin family members during the formation of the actomyosin interface.
source: These differences are likely to contribute to distinct interactions with the positively charged loop-2 and other actin-binding elements in the motor domain of myosin family members during the formation of the actomyosin interface.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and chemical analysis.

claim: Actin isoform-specific interfaces may be further diversified by differential N-terminal processing of β-actin, PTMs, and alternatively spliced myosin motors.
source: Actin isoform-specific interfaces may be further diversified by differential N-terminal processing of β-actin, PTMs, and alternatively spliced myosin motors (Varland et al., 2019; Müller et al., 2013; Arnesen et al., 2018; Terman and Kashina, 2013; Heissler and Manstein, 2011; Sheff and Rubenstein, 1989; Solomon and Rubenstein, 1985).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations.

claim: The Nt-acetylated N-termini of actin isoforms would likely be more efficient to establish electrostatic interactions with the positively charged loop-2 of myosin.
source: For example, the Nt-acetylated N-termini of actin isoforms would likely be more efficient to establish electrostatic interactions with the positively charged loop-2 of myosin, while the addition of a positive charge to the N-terminus of β-actin through arginylation may weaken the interaction.
evidence: This is speculation based on chemical properties.

claim: The addition of a positive charge to the N-terminus of β-actin through arginylation may weaken the interaction with myosin.
source: For example, the Nt-acetylated N-termini of actin isoforms would likely be more efficient to establish electrostatic interactions with the positively charged loop-2 of myosin, while the addition of a positive charge to the N-terminus of β-actin through arginylation may weaken the interaction.
evidence: This is speculation based on chemical properties.

claim: The actin N-terminus has been shown previously to interact with numerous ABPs.
source: While we focused our comparative structural analysis on the interaction between actin isoforms with myosin motors, the actin N-terminus has been shown previously to interact with numerous ABPs (Arnesen et al., 2018; Cook et al., 1993; Abe et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The proposed isoform-specific interaction mechanisms that stem from the different conformations of the N-termini extend to ABPs.
source: Therefore, we speculate that the proposed isoform-specific interaction mechanisms that stem from the different conformations of the N-termini extend to ABPs.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural analysis.

claim: The structures of single-isotype, post-translationally modified bare skeletal muscle α-actin, cardiac muscle α-actin, ß-actin, and γ-actin reveal general principles, similarities, and differences between isoforms.
source: Collectively, the structures of single-isotype, post-translationally modified bare skeletal muscle α-actin, cardiac muscle α-actin, ß-actin, and γ-actin reveal general principles, similarities, and differences between isoforms.
evidence: This is a summary of the structural findings.

claim: The structures complement the repertoire of known actin structures and allow for a comprehensive understanding of in vitro and in vivo functions of actin isoforms.
source: They complement the repertoire of known actin structures and allow for a comprehensive understanding of in vitro and in vivo functions of actin isoforms.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the contribution of the work.

claim: Rabbit skeletal muscle α-actin (UniProt ID: P68135) was prepared from acetone powder.
source: Rabbit skeletal muscle α-actin (UniProt ID: P68135) was prepared from acetone powder (Pel-Freez Biologicals, Rogers, AR, USA) as described earlier (Heissler et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the experimental method.

claim: Cardiac muscle α-actin (UniProt ID: Q3ZC07) was prepared from the left ventricle of a bovine heart.
source: Cardiac muscle α-actin (UniProt ID: Q3ZC07) was prepared from the left ventricle of a bovine heart (local butcher) as described for skeletal muscle α-actin.
evidence: This describes the experimental method.

claim: At the amino acid level, rabbit skeletal muscle α-actin and bovine cardiac muscle α-actin are identical to the respective human proteins.
source: At the amino acid level, both proteins are identical to the respective human proteins.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison.

claim: The actin filament is composed of G-actin (42 kDa) protomers that are oriented in the same direction.
source: The actin filament itself is composed of G-actin (42 kDa) protomers that are oriented in the same direction (Holmes et al., 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Each actin protomer folds into four subdomains that are referred to as SD1–SD4.
source: Each protomer folds into four subdomains that are referred to as SD1–SD4 (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Kabsch et al., 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: SD1 and SD2 form the outer domain, and SD3 and SD4 form the inner domain.
source: SD1 and SD2 form the outer domain, and SD3 and SD4 form the inner domain (Figure 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: The domain arrangement results in the formation of two clefts – the nucleotide-binding cleft and the barbed end groove.
source: This domain arrangement results in the formation of two clefts – the nucleotide-binding cleft and the barbed end groove (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Pollard, 2016; Dominguez and Holmes, 2011; Merino et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The nucleotide-binding cleft between SD2 and SD4 harbors the active site that is occupied by Mg2+·ADP in the structures.
source: The nucleotide-binding cleft between SD2 and SD4 harbors the active site that is occupied by Mg2+·ADP in our structures (Figure 1E, Figure 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: The barbed end groove between SD1 and SD3 represents a major binding interface for myosins and ABPs.
source: The barbed end groove between SD1 and SD3 represents a major binding interface for myosins and ABPs (von der Ecken et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The barbed end groove mediates longitudinal interfaces within the actin filament.
source: It further mediates longitudinal interfaces within the actin filament.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: SD2 and SD4 of an actin protomer are at the pointed end, and SD1 and SD3 are at the barbed end.
source: SD2 and SD4 of an actin protomer are at the pointed end, and SD1 and SD3 are at the barbed end (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Pollard, 2016; Dominguez and Holmes, 2011; Merino et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The longitudinal interface between two adjacent actin protomers involves the extended D-loop located in SD2 of one actin protomer that interacts with amino acids located in SD1 and SD3 of another protomer.
source: The longitudinal interface between two adjacent actin protomers involves the extended D-loop located in SD2 of one actin protomer that interacts with amino acids located in SD1 and SD3 of another protomer.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: Both the N- and C-terminus of the actin protomer are in SD1.
source: Both the N- and C-terminus of the actin protomer are in SD1 (Pollard, 2016; Dominguez and Holmes, 2011; Merino et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The actin reconstructions show the characteristic double-stranded actin helix with a helical rise of ~27.6 Å to 28 Å and a helical twist of ~–166.5° to –168°.
source: Consistent with the high sequence conservation across actin isoforms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C), our reconstructions show the characteristic double-stranded actin helix with a helical rise of ~27.6 Å to 28 Å and a helical twist of ~–166.5° to –168° (Figure 1A–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) that has been observed in numerous previous structural studies, including previous high-resolution cryo-EM studies (Holmes et al., 1990; Chou and Pollard, 2019; Mei et al., 2020; Oda et al., 2009; Egelman et al., 1982; Ali et al., 2022; Fujii et al., 2010; Galkin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: For ß-actin and γ-actin, the entire N-terminus starting from amino acids D1 and E1, respectively, could be resolved.
source: For ß-actin and γ-actin, we could resolve the entire N-terminus starting from amino acids D1 and E1, respectively.
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data analysis.

claim: For skeletal muscle α-actin and cardiac muscle α-actin, the N-terminus starting from amino acids E4 and D2, respectively, could be resolved.
source: For skeletal muscle α-actin and cardiac muscle α-actin, we could resolve the N-terminus starting from amino acids E4 and D2, respectively.
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data analysis.

claim: The lack of resolvable density for the very first amino acid of cardiac muscle α-actin and the first three amino acids of skeletal muscle α-actin may be attributed to a nonuniform PTM pattern of native actin isoforms prepared from muscle.
source: The lack of resolvable density for the very first amino acid of cardiac muscle α-actin and the first three amino acids of skeletal muscle α-actin may be attributed to a nonuniform PTM pattern of native actin isoforms prepared from muscle compared to our recombinant nonmuscle actin isoforms with uniform PTM pattern in that the entire N-terminus region could be resolved (Figure 1E, Figure 1—videos 1–5).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of recombinant and native actins.

claim: Nt-acetylation and H72/H73 methylation are highly conserved in vertebrate actins.
source: Nt-acetylation and H72/H73 methylation are highly conserved in vertebrate actins and therefore expected to be present in most if not all previous structures of filamentous F-actin.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge.

claim: The methylated H72/H73 has been only recently resolved in the structure of skeletal muscle α-actin.
source: However, the methylated H72/H73 has been only recently resolved in the structure of skeletal muscle α-actin (Chou and Pollard, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The high resolution of the structures allowed resolution of the methylated H72/H73.
source: The high resolution of our structures allowed us to resolve the methylated H72/H73.
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data analysis.

claim: The acetylated N-termini in filamentous ß-actin and γ-actin could be resolved.
source: Furthermore, we could resolve the acetylated N-termini in filamentous ß-actin and γ-actin.
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data analysis.
